ops.new_text: \rev{A master's project that clustered whole 12-lead records reported misleading numbers, and its conclusion is the starting point of this study. The project flattened each record into a long vector, compressed it with a dense autoencoder, and clustered the code. Its report gave a high cluster purity, the share of the majority class inside the clusters, and a silhouette score near 0.89, an index of cluster compactness computed without labels. The purity equalled the majority-class proportion in every setting, however, and the silhouette was measured on a degenerate solution in which almost all points fell into a single cluster. The project concluded that the difficulty lies in processing the raw signal rather than in the clustering step. We test that conclusion under chance-corrected evaluation, with a supervised ceiling for each representation.}

ops.rationale: Split into a paragraph on separability and clusterability and one on the closest benchmark (F15); defines linear separability, clusterability and the probe at first use (F1, F2); replaces 'this axis' (F3) and the vague 'differ notably' by what the source reports (F22); takes the one point only the deleted Related-work paragraph held, the source's note on earlier benchmarks (F9); drops 'cluster-separability' (F1).
ops.new_text:
\rev{A representation can carry information about a label and still fail to cluster by it. Linear separability is how well a linear classifier trained on the labels recovers them from the representation. Clusterability is a distinct property: how well an unsupervised partition of the representation agrees with the labels. A representation may place the discriminative direction far from its dominant axes of variation. A supervised probe, a classifier trained on the labels, then recovers the label while an unsupervised partition does not. In self-supervised image models, the hidden-layer outputs of the projector scored worse on clustering metrics than the encodings. A single linear layer separates the two, and both reach nearly the same linear-probe accuracy \cite{sslclustering2025}. We treat this distinction as background rather than as a finding.}

\rev{For the ECG, how the common representation families compare on separability and clusterability under chance-corrected metrics has not been measured. The most directly related work benchmarks several ECG foundation models against one another \cite{lookingbeyond2026}. Pooled over 12-lead datasets with PTB-XL among them, it analyses how far their embeddings group by clinical label and by dataset. It notes that the earlier benchmarks it reviews included no representation-wise evaluation and focused on performance in downstream tasks. It adds no hand-crafted features, and its datasets do not include the MIT-BIH database. A comparison with hand-crafted features matters because they are interpretable and need no training, and MIT-BIH adds a beat-morphology task to the rhythm task of PTB-XL.}

ops.new_text:
\paragraph{Unsupervised ECG and representations.} Hand-crafted features built from
RR-interval irregularity and beat morphology encode the defining signatures of common
arrhythmias and underpin decades of automatic analysis \cite{hrvstandards1996,dechazal2004}.
Tensor and wavelet decompositions have been combined with spectral clustering for
unsupervised 12-lead classification \cite{wavelettensorecg2018}. \rev{A reconstruction autoencoder is trained only to reproduce its input, and its objective holds no term that separates the classes. Its bottleneck may therefore encode a class without arranging it into clusters, as the conv-AE of this study does (Section~\ref{sec:results}).} \rev{Contrastive self-supervised methods for the ECG preceded the foundation models below. CLOCS \cite{clocs2021} builds on patient- and lead-level invariances, and 3KG \cite{threekg2021} on physiologically motivated augmentations. Contrastive predictive coding for 12-lead ECG adapts a self-supervised method from other domains \cite{mehari2022ssl}.} Self-supervised and foundation models for
ECG, such as HuBERT-ECG \cite{hubertecg2024} and ECGFounder \cite{ecgfounder2024}, learn
general representations from millions of recordings and are now evaluated as frozen
feature extractors.

\rev{We compare four representation families: raw flattening, the conv-AE, hand-crafted features and frozen foundation-model embeddings. Raw flattening and the conv-AE encode signal energy, through the sample amplitudes and the reconstruction objective. The foundation-model embeddings place each record in a feature space fixed by large-scale pretraining, and the hand-crafted features encode the quantities that define the classes. The wavelet-tensor and spectral-clustering method of \cite{wavelettensorecg2018} addresses a related unsupervised goal with a different (tensor) representation, and we leave a tensor representation to future work.}

ops.rationale: The 41-word sentence is split into the definition of the two indices, the reason they are zero for one cluster, and the claim that they are the appropriate headline metrics.
ops.new_text:
\paragraph{Clustering evaluation.} Cluster purity is not chance-corrected: assigning
every point to the majority class attains a purity equal to that class's prevalence.
\rev{The adjusted Rand index \cite{hubertarabie1985} and adjusted mutual information \cite{vinh2010} are external, chance-corrected indices. Both are zero for a one-cluster solution, since its Rand index equals its expectation and its mutual information with the classes is zero. This property makes them the appropriate headline metrics.} Internal indices such as the silhouette
\cite{rousseeuw1987} measure compactness in the embedding being clustered and can be
maximised by degenerate solutions, so they require cluster-size sanity checks.

ops.new_text: \paragraph{PTB-XL.} \rev{We used PTB-XL, a public 12-lead database, in its version 1.0.3, which holds 21\,799 records from 18\,869 patients. The paper that describes the database \cite{ptbxl2020} reports 21\,837 records from 18\,885 patients. Each record holds one 10\,s signal of twelve leads, called a strip below. Rhythm labels were taken from the SCP-ECG (Standard Communications Protocol for Computer-Assisted Electrocardiography) statements. The SR-versus-AF cohort used as positives all records carrying an AF statement, AFIB (atrial fibrillation) or AFLT (atrial flutter), so atrial flutter records were counted as AF positives. Sinus-rhythm records without any AF statement served as controls.} PTB-XL encodes rhythm statements at a likelihood of zero meaning ``present'', \rev{so a presence-based rule was required, since a confidence threshold would discard every SR record. We drew a balanced, patient-disjoint cohort of 2\,542 records (1\,282 SR, 1\,260 AF), so the majority-class baseline is 0.504. Records were taken from the \mbox{100\,Hz} release of the database as signals of 1000 samples by 12 leads. No filtering, resampling or rescaling was applied before each representation's own preprocessing, so every representation started from the same signal. We chose the lead set for each representation separately, and the description of each representation below states it. Every fold of the evaluation was drawn by patient, and no patient contributed records to both classes.}

ops.new_text: \rev{Tolerances and iteration caps of the clusterers were the scikit-learn defaults, and no early stopping was imposed on them. Ward agglomerative clustering and HDBSCAN are deterministic given the input matrix, so each was fitted once rather than once per seed. The conv-AE was trained with Adam at a learning rate of \mbox{$10^{-3}$} and batch size 64, for at most 50 epochs on a 90/10 train/validation split. Training stopped when the validation reconstruction error had not improved for eight epochs, and the best-validation weights were kept. The two foundation models were used as frozen feature extractors with their published weights unchanged. HuBERT-ECG was mean-pooled over time from its last hidden layer at batch size 64, and the globally average-pooled 1024-dimensional feature layer of ECGFounder was taken at batch size 32.}

ops.new_text: \rev{HDBSCAN labels records it does not assign to any dense region as noise, and the metrics treated that label in two ways. ARI, AMI, NMI, V-measure and Fowlkes-Mallows received the prediction unchanged, so the noise records formed one further group of their own and were charged against the agreement with the true partition. Purity and the silhouette were computed on the assigned records only, because neither is defined for a set that is not a cluster, and the purity denominator stayed the full cohort. Noise records were never dropped from the evaluation and never reassigned to a nearest cluster. This treatment is why HDBSCAN gave the lowest ARI of the five clusterers, or shared it, on every representation. At this minimum cluster size it assigned a minority of the cohort on the representations that cluster well, and on the matrices of raw flattening, the conv-AE and HuBERT-ECG it labelled the entire cohort as noise, which leaves one group and an ARI of exactly zero.}

ops.rationale: The global initialisation of the centroids becomes its own sentence placed before the rounds, and the aggregation rule keeps its own sentence; the rest is unchanged.
ops.new_text: \rev{To probe deployment under data siloing we used federated $k$-means, in which the server averages the site centroids with weights, as FedAvg averages locally trained models \cite{fedavg2017}. The 2\,542 records were partitioned, patient-grouped, across ten simulated sites, either independently and identically distributed (IID) or with class proportions drawn from a Dirichlet distribution so that sites differed sharply in arrhythmia prevalence (non-IID). The Dirichlet concentration was 0.3, applied per class over the ten sites, and any site left holding fewer records than clusters was dropped. Feature scaling was fitted once on the full representation matrix before partitioning, so the federation concerned the clustering step alone. Separate sites would not share these pooled statistics, a limitation taken up in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}. Federated clustering consisted of fifteen aggregation rounds of three local Lloyd iterations per site. Before the first round the centroids were initialised globally from two randomly drawn records. In each round the server replaced each centroid by the mean of the site centroids, weighted by the number of records each site assigned to it. Both settings were repeated over ten seeds, with the site partition and the centroid initialisation redrawn at each seed. We report the global ARI relative to centralized clustering of the same representation.}

ops.rationale: 'Fell on some representations, such as HuBERT-ECG' is replaced by the spectral ARI on HuBERT-ECG against the other two seeded clusterers, the one representation where Table 2 shows the fall (F22); the chance outcome takes the term 'chance level' (F1).
ops.new_text: \rev{On PTB-XL the spread of ARI across representations was larger than the spread across clustering algorithms within a strong representation, so the representation decided the outcome (Table~\ref{tab:main} and Fig.~\ref{fig:heatmap}). ECGFounder clustered best (ARI up to 0.885 with $k$-means), the hand-crafted features were competitive (0.711 with agglomerative clustering), HuBERT-ECG was weak (0.195), and raw flattening and the conv-AE clustered at chance level (ARI $\approx 0$). Among the clusterers, HDBSCAN labelled most points as noise and underperformed throughout. Spectral clustering reached 0.016 on HuBERT-ECG, against 0.174 for $k$-means and 0.195 for the Gaussian mixture on the same representation. A poorly connected nearest-neighbour affinity graph is a possible cause, and the connectivity of the graph was not measured. Both clusterers are reported with the settings given in Section~\ref{sec:methods}, and their parameters were not adjusted to the outcome.}

With adjusted mutual information for $K$ from 2 to 8, ECGFounder led at every $K$, from 0.825 at $K=2$ to a minimum of 0.441 at $K=7$ and 0.450 at $K=8$. ops.new_text: \rev{The position of each representation followed from two things: how much of the label its space holds, which the supervised ceiling in the last column of Table~\ref{tab:main} measures, and where in the space that label lies. The hand-crafted representation is 16-dimensional and each coordinate is a quantity by which the classes are defined, RR irregularity and P-wave presence. Its ceiling was 0.942 and an unsupervised partition recovered 0.711. ECGFounder had the highest ceiling, 0.983, recovered the most, 0.885, and led at every $K$ from 2 to 8, so the rhythm split is one of the larger sources of variation in its 1024 dimensions. HuBERT-ECG had almost the same ceiling as the hand-crafted features, 0.899, and recovered 0.195. This difference between the two foundation models matches the report of \cite{lookingbeyond2026} that some ECG foundation embeddings organise by clinical label and others by dataset.}

ops.new_text: \rev{Raw flattening and the conv-AE both clustered at chance level under all five clusterers, for different reasons. The conv-AE reached a supervised ceiling of 0.678, the class information that its bottleneck kept although it was trained only to reconstruct the signal, and its best clustering ARI was 0.008. Raw flattening reached a ceiling of 0.519 against a majority of 0.504, so a linear probe found almost no label in the 1992-dimensional vector. Two causes may explain this linear failure. The coordinates are amplitudes at fixed sample offsets, and no fixed offset falls on the same part of the cardiac cycle in two records. The vector also has nearly as many coordinates (1992) as the cohort has records (2\,542), which leaves a linear probe few records per coefficient. A random forest on the same vector reached 0.714, so a non-linear readout recovered label information that the linear probe missed. This is consistent with both causes, and the benchmark does not separate them.}

ECGFounder and the hand-crafted features were high on both properties. The conv-AE and HuBERT-ECG were separable but not clusterable, and raw flattening, with a linear ceiling barely above the majority baseline, was low on both. We read the gap of these weaker embeddings as one of geometry: their discriminative information exists but does not lie along their dominant axes of variation.}

ops.new_text: \rev{A non-linear probe showed that this gap is not an artefact of a linear probe. A random forest on raw flattening reached accuracy 0.714, well above its linear ceiling of 0.519 and far above its clustering ARI of 0.000, so even a non-linear decoder recovered a label that clustering did not. The same probe gave 0.951 on the hand-crafted features, 0.983 on ECGFounder and 0.825 on HuBERT-ECG. On ECGFounder the two probes agreed to three decimals, the linear ceiling at 0.9831 and the random forest at 0.9835. On the two representations that cluster well the non-linear probe therefore added little over the linear ceiling (0.951 against 0.942 for the hand-crafted features), so their clustering is not held back by information that only a non-linear readout reaches. ops.rationale: The general claim that no single direction separates the classes is limited to the one direction tested, the fitted linear discriminant, and hedged.
ops.new_text: \rev{HuBERT-ECG showed the largest gain. One direction estimated from other patients recovered more than three times what its own 768 dimensions yield unsupervised, so the class information is present, transfers across patients, and lies away from the directions that dominate the embedding. ECGFounder gained almost nothing, because its dominant axes already carry the split. The conv-AE rose off chance and stopped far short of its ceiling of 0.678, so its class structure is both off-axis and diffuse. Raw flattening did not move at all, which distinguishes its failure from that of HuBERT-ECG. The one direction tested, the linear discriminant estimated from other patients, did not separate its classes, so the label information that the random forest recovered from it appears not to lie along that direction.}

ops.rationale: 'Internal indices misled here' is limited to the silhouette, the one internal index measured, and states what it did; the evidence that follows is unchanged.
ops.new_text: \rev{The silhouette, the one internal index we measured, rated a degenerate solution above a solution that recovered the classes. Raw flattening with agglomerative clustering attained a silhouette of 0.81 while the ARI was 0.000 and its largest cluster held a fraction of 1.00 of the cohort. That fraction is rounded to two decimals, so at most 12 of the 2\,542 records lay outside the largest cluster. The hand-crafted representation, which recovered the classes (ARI 0.711, balanced clusters), had a \emph{lower} silhouette of 0.28. Fig.~\ref{fig:trap} plots 157 clustering solutions, which cover 22 of the 25 representation-by-clusterer cells. The three cells left out are HDBSCAN fits that labelled the whole cohort as noise, for which the silhouette is undefined. Across the plotted solutions the degenerate one-cluster solutions attained a high silhouette at zero ARI. A degenerate one-cluster solution maximises compactness while carrying no class information. This is the artefact behind the original project's silhouette of 0.89, and it is why chance-corrected external metrics, read together with cluster-size sanity checks, are necessary.}

ops.rationale: The one untested cause is limited to the hand-crafted features and stated as untested, and the text says that it does not account for the drop of ECGFounder, whose coordinates are not arrhythmic quantities.
ops.new_text: \rev{The mean ARI over clusterers depended on the feature scaling. For the hand-crafted features it was 0.629 under standard scaling and 0.606 under power scaling, but fell to 0.360 under robust scaling and 0.229 under quantile scaling. The effect was not confined to the hand-crafted features: the mean ARI of ECGFounder dropped from 0.866 under standard scaling to 0.093 under robust scaling. One possible cause for the hand-crafted features, which we did not test, is that robust scaling leaves the heavy tails of the arrhythmic RR statistics unbounded. A few outlying records could then dominate Euclidean distance. That explanation rests on arrhythmic quantities, which the coordinates of ECGFounder are not, so it does not account for the drop of ECGFounder, whose cause we did not examine. Feature scaling should therefore be reported in ECG clustering, together with a sweep over scaling methods.}

ops.new_text: \rev{Under the 9:1 SR:AF class imbalance the hand-crafted features overtook ECGFounder. At this natural-like ratio (majority 0.90) the ARI of every representation above chance level fell. A 10\% minority class gives a clusterer fewer records from which to form a cluster of its own. The hand-crafted features retained the most structure over the ten seeds (ARI 0.265 [0.250, 0.280], AMI 0.245 [0.233, 0.257]), against ARI 0.063 [0.061, 0.065] and AMI 0.148 [0.143, 0.152] for ECGFounder, with no overlap between the two ARI intervals. By ARI its partition agreed with the classes on record pairs beyond chance and about as well as that of ECGFounder, and by AMI it carried less information about them. ops.new_text: \rev{Of the five representations, ECGFounder, which clustered best, took the longest to compute per record (Table~\ref{tab:cost}). Its extraction took fifteen times as long as the hand-crafted extraction. The hand-crafted features also carry no learned parameters. Clustering itself was negligible everywhere, under \mbox{0.3\,s} for the whole cohort at any of the five dimensionalities, so the cost of a representation is the cost of extracting it.}

ops.rationale: The rule for imbalanced or siloed data is scoped to the two stress settings tested (F7); 'come within reach' is replaced by 0.711 against 0.885 (F22); the restating close is cut (F17); the evidence for the lead clause moves here from the next paragraph, whose first sentence was a one-line summary covering a second idea (F11).
ops.new_text: \rev{The practical reading is a decision rule for the two tasks evaluated here: SR-versus-AF rhythm separation on PTB-XL and N-vs-V beat morphology on MIT-BIH. If the data are balanced and come in the 12-lead format that the tested version of ECGFounder takes, ECGFounder gives the best unsupervised separation here. We tested two stress settings, a 9:1 SR:AF imbalance and a simulated non-IID federation over ten sites judged by its worst site draw. In both, the 16 hand-crafted features were the better choice, and they are also preferable where interpretability or low dimensionality matters. On balanced PTB-XL data their best ARI was 0.711 against 0.885 for ECGFounder. Under the 9:1 imbalance they overtook it (ARI 0.265 against 0.063), and over the site draws of non-IID federation they varied far less. The hand-crafted features remain the choice when the leads on hand are not the twelve that the tested foundation-model versions take. Neither of those versions could embed the 2-lead MIT-BIH beats, whereas the hand-crafted design carried over to them through a separate beat-level feature set of the same kind. The cost comparison of Table~\ref{tab:cost} supports the same rule. The representation that retains the most ARI under both stressors is also the less costly of the two to compute, and its 16 coordinates are clinical quantities that a reader can inspect for each record.}

ops.rationale: The one-line opener is cut and the lead evidence moved to the decision-rule paragraph, so this paragraph covers one idea and opens on it (F11); the claim on the conv-AE is scoped to the one configuration tested, stated as the study's scope (F6); 'indistinguishable from predicting the majority class' takes 'chance level' (F1).
ops.new_text: \rev{Raw flattening and the conv-AE, including the design of the original project, recovered little of the arrhythmia classes without labels on either task. On PTB-XL both clustered at chance level under all five clusterers. On MIT-BIH their best ARIs were 0.127 for the conv-AE and 0.049 for the raw beat window, against 0.783 for the beat-morphology features. The statement on the conv-AE covers the one configuration tested, an autoencoder with a 32-unit bottleneck trained to reconstruct its input. Other bottleneck sizes, architectures and training objectives lie outside the scope of this study.}

ops.rationale: 'cluster-separability analysis' and 'hand-crafted axis' take the paper's terms (F1); the one-sentence paragraph on existing tools is removed because it repeats the Introduction and the Methods, and the key sslclustering2025 stays cited in the Introduction (F9).
'foundation-model axis' and 'foundation arm' take the one name of that family (F1); the 48-word sentence is split into the reason the two models suit a frozen benchmark and the way they differ (F18).
ops.new_text:
\rev{We limited the foundation-model embeddings to two models, selected for the reasons that follow rather than by a survey of the field.
HuBERT-ECG and ECGFounder both publish weights that load into a frozen feature extractor
without fine-tuning, which a benchmark of frozen embeddings requires. They also differ
in pretraining objective and architecture: HuBERT-ECG is a self-supervised transformer
\cite{hubertecg2024}, and ECGFounder is a convolutional model pretrained on more than ten million
recordings \cite{ecgfounder2024}. Their clustering ARIs are far apart, 0.885 against 0.195, so the two do not behave as one kind of embedding. What this limit does to the conclusions is to scope them: every statement here about a foundation model
is a statement about one of these two, the deployment comparison is between the hand-crafted
features and ECGFounder specifically, and none of it extends to ECG foundation models as a
class. A further model that clusters as well as ECGFounder on balanced data would leave the
results reported here unchanged, and would have to be measured again under imbalance and
under federation before the deployment reading could be extended to it.}

ops.rationale: The decision not to include other models takes 'we' (F24); the 'thus' sentence becomes a clause of the sentence before it (F12); 'arm' and 'raw representations' take the paper's terms (F1).
ops.new_text: \rev{We evaluated two foundation models. We did not include others, among them ECG-FM, whose embeddings the benchmark of \cite{lookingbeyond2026} reported to separate clinical labels. Neither of the two was evaluated on MIT-BIH, for the reason given in Section~\ref{sec:methods}, so the MIT-BIH comparison covers the beat-morphology features, the conv-AE and the raw beat window only. The input of one of the two was also shorter than that of every other representation. HuBERT-ECG received the first \mbox{5\,s} of each \mbox{10\,s} strip and so saw fewer RR intervals, while every other representation saw the full strip. The shorter window is therefore an alternative explanation for its weak clustering, beside the off-axis geometry measured in Section~\ref{sec:results} and the organisation by dataset that \cite{lookingbeyond2026} reported for some foundation models.}

ops.rationale: The uncited clinical claim that flutter need not show an irregular rhythm is replaced by what the study can state: its reading rests on AF being defined by an irregular rhythm, and it did not check the flutter records for that irregularity.
ops.new_text: \rev{The AF class of the rhythm task also counted atrial flutter records as positives. The cohort took every record with an AFIB or AFLT statement as AF (Section~\ref{sec:methods}). The reading of Section~\ref{sec:intro} rests on AF being defined by an irregular rhythm. We did not check whether the flutter records share that irregularity, so those records may sit closer to the SR class than the AF definition suggests. The ARI of every representation was computed against these labels, and no result here separates the flutter records from the fibrillation records. Removing the AFLT records, or giving them a class of their own, would show how far they move the ARI of each representation.}

ops.rationale: 'by a wide margin' is replaced by the largest change the Results report, ECGFounder from 0.866 to 0.093; the rest is unchanged.
ops.new_text: \rev{The federated study is a simulation on a single physical dataset, and no multi-institution deployment was evaluated. Its only control on heterogeneity is the Dirichlet concentration, which moves class prevalence across sites and nothing else, and the spread that alone produces is already wide: over the ten redrawn non-IID partitions ECGFounder ranged from chance to 0.881, while the hand-crafted features stayed between 0.455 and 0.643. Feature scaling in the simulation also used statistics pooled over all sites, which separate institutions would not share. The choice of scaling changed the centralized results, lowering the mean ARI of ECGFounder from 0.866 under standard scaling to 0.093 under robust scaling (Section~\ref{sec:results}). Device vendor, lead placement, population case mix and local labelling practice also differ between hospitals and are absent from the simulation. Settling their effect needs recordings held at several institutions, clustered under a federated protocol with the site of origin retained as a variable, which was not available for this study.}

ops.rationale: The imbalance claim is limited to the one ratio tested, 9:1 SR:AF (F7); 'sit at chance' takes 'clustered at chance level' and raw flattening its one name (F1); the federation results move to the past tense of the sentence before them.
ops.new_text: \rev{For unsupervised arrhythmia structure in the ECG, the choice of representation moved clustering ARI further than the choice of clustering algorithm on the two tasks evaluated, and chance-corrected external evaluation was required to see it. On balanced PTB-XL data ECGFounder, pretrained on more than ten million recordings \cite{ecgfounder2024}, leads. Under the one class imbalance tested, a 9:1 SR:AF ratio, 16 interpretable hand-crafted features overtook it. Under simulated federation across ten heterogeneous sites they retained 0.92 of their centralized ARI against 0.69 and never fell below 0.455 over the ten site draws. On PTB-XL raw flattening and the conv-AE clustered at chance level under all five clusterers. Internal indices and feature scaling are not neutral choices and must be reported. Whether these results hold for multi-class arrhythmia cohorts, for other foundation models and for a real multi-institution federation is open.}
